name: Johann Sebastian Bach
alt: An oil painting of an older man in 18th-century dress with a powdered wig, holding a rolled sheet of music.
facts: He wrote a brand-new piece of music almost every single week for years while working as a church choirmaster in Germany.
He had over 20 children, and several of them grew up to become composers too.
He once walked roughly 250 miles, mostly on foot, just to hear another organist play.

name: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
alt: An oil painting of a young man with powdered hair and a red coat, gazing slightly sideways.
facts: He was composing his own music before he turned 5 years old.
He secretly copied down a piece of church music from memory after hearing it performed just once, even though copying it was forbidden.
He could compose an entire piece in his head before ever putting pen to paper.

name: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina
alt: An old engraved portrait of a bearded man in a long dark robe.
facts: He spent most of his career as the music director at one of the most important churches in Rome.
His smooth, calm style of choral writing became the model that church composers were told to imitate for centuries afterward.
Legend credits him with saving elaborate church polyphony from being banned outright by leaders who worried the words were getting lost in the music.

name: George Frideric Handel
alt: An oil painting of a heavyset man in a powdered wig and dark coat, facing forward.
facts: He wrote one of his most famous works, about the life of Jesus, in only about three weeks.
He moved from Germany to England and became so beloved there that he's buried in a hall reserved for the country's national heroes.
Audiences have stood up during one particular chorus of his ever since a king supposedly did the same.

name: Antonio Vivaldi
alt: An old engraving of a man with curly red hair playing a violin.
facts: He was ordained as a priest but became so famous for music that people nicknamed him after his red hair instead of his collar.
He taught violin at an orphanage for girls for most of his career, writing much of his most famous music for his students to perform.
He wrote more than 500 concertos, including a famous set inspired by the four seasons of the year.

name: Gabriel Fauré
alt: A black-and-white photo of an older man with a thick white mustache and beard.
facts: He spent over 15 years as the organist at a grand church in Paris while writing music on the side.
One of his most famous choral works was written for a funeral, but he said he wanted it to feel peaceful rather than frightening.
He eventually became the director of one of France's top music schools, after years of supporting himself mainly by teaching piano.

name: Franz Schubert
alt: An oil painting of a young man with curly hair and small round glasses.
facts: He wrote more than 600 songs in a lifetime that lasted only 31 years.
He set a famous prayer to music so beautifully that it's still sung at weddings and funerals two centuries later.
He was so shy about sharing his own music that many of his greatest works weren't performed in public until after he had died.

name: Tomás Luis de Victoria
alt: An old engraved portrait of a man in a plain clerical collar.
facts: He left his home country to study for the priesthood in Rome, where he also became one of the leading composers of his time.
He spent his final years as chaplain to a dowager empress, writing sacred music for her private chapel.
His choral music is still sung in churches today, written entirely for voices alone, with no instruments at all.

name: Gregorio Allegri
alt: An old painting of a man in dark religious robes with a white collar.
facts: He wrote a piece for the Sistine Chapel that the Pope decreed could never be copied or performed anywhere else.
For over a century, the only way to hear his most famous work was to travel to Rome during Holy Week.
A teenage visitor is famously said to have broken the secrecy by listening to it twice and writing the whole thing down from memory.

name: Johannes Brahms
alt: A black-and-white photo of an older man with a long white beard and round glasses.
facts: He took over 20 years to finish his first symphony because he felt so much pressure to live up to earlier German composers.
He wrote a large-scale choral work to comfort the living after losing his mother and his mentor in the same year, rather than focusing on judgment day like older requiems did.
He had a reputation for being gruff and blunt in person, even though his music is full of warmth.

name: Giuseppe Verdi
alt: A black-and-white photo of an older man with a thick white beard, looking off to the side.
facts: He's best known for his operas, but he also wrote a dramatic Requiem so theatrical that one famous conductor called it 'an opera in church robes.'
He grew up the son of a village innkeeper and almost failed the entrance exam to the music conservatory in Milan.
He donated much of his fortune to build a retirement home for musicians who had fallen on hard times.

name: Charles Gounod
alt: An old sepia-toned photo of a man with long gray hair and a thick beard.
facts: He once seriously considered becoming a priest before deciding to dedicate his life to music instead.
His most famous melody was written as a tribute layered on top of a keyboard piece written by another composer a century earlier.
He composed an opera based on a famous tragic love story that's still one of the most performed operas in the world.

name: César Franck
alt: A black-and-white photo of an elderly man with glasses and a long white beard.
facts: He worked for over 30 years as the organist of a single Paris church, playing for services nearly every week.
He didn't become widely famous as a composer until very late in life, after decades known mainly as a teacher.
One of his most beloved pieces was written simply enough for an amateur church choir to sing, using just voice, harp, cello, and organ.

name: Maurice Duruflé
alt: A black-and-white photo of a young man with dark, neatly combed hair.
facts: He was such a perfectionist that he published only a small handful of works in his entire career, revising pieces for years before letting them go.
He based one of his most famous works almost entirely on ancient chant melodies that monks have sung for over a thousand years.
He worked for over four decades as the organist of the same Paris church, a job he only gave up after a serious car accident.

name: John Rutter
alt: A color photo of an older man with white hair, smiling warmly.
facts: He turned down a job leading a famous choir at Cambridge so he'd have more time to compose.
Choirs around the world perform his music every December, even though his most famous Christmas carols are entirely original, not old folk tunes.
He started his own small choir specifically so he could hear his own choral music performed exactly the way he imagined it.

name: Eric Whitacre
alt: A color photo of a man with short, light-colored hair against a dark background.
facts: He didn't learn to read music until college, after starting out as a music major who could barely play piano.
He brought together thousands of singers from dozens of countries who had never met in person, using nothing but webcams and the internet.
He says the spark that made him fall in love with choral music was joining a college choir almost by accident.

name: Ralph Vaughan Williams
alt: A black-and-white photo of a middle-aged man with thick eyebrows and tousled hair.
facts: He traveled the English countryside with a notebook, collecting old folk songs before they could be forgotten, and wove their melodies into his own music.
He helped edit a hymn book still used in churches today, and wrote one of its best-loved tunes himself.
He kept composing well into his 80s, finishing a symphony just a couple of years before he died.

name: Felix Mendelssohn
alt: An oil painting of a young man with dark curly hair and sideburns.
facts: He was such a musical prodigy that he wrote a piece still performed today by the time he was 17.
He's credited with reviving interest in a much earlier composer's work after organizing a performance of a piece that had been mostly forgotten for about a century.
He composed the tune millions of people sing every December without realizing it first celebrated the invention of the printing press, not Christmas.

name: Hildegard of Bingen
alt: An illuminated manuscript painting of a robed woman seated in an arched doorway, with flames above her head, dictating to a monk.
facts: She was running a religious community by her early 30s and is one of the earliest composers in history whose name we actually know.
She wrote her own original chant melodies, an unusually creative thing for someone in her position at the time, when most music was anonymous.
She also wrote about medicine, theology, and natural science, and described visions she said she'd had since childhood.

name: Claudio Monteverdi
alt: An oil painting of a man with a long gray beard, dressed in dark robes.
facts: He helped invent a brand-new kind of musical storytelling that eventually grew into what we now call opera.
He wrote an enormous setting of evening prayers that calls for multiple choirs, soloists, and instrumental groups all at once.
Late in life, after losing his wife, he became a priest while continuing to compose some of his most ambitious music.
